This section examines Chapter 7 — How the
experimental standard

matured (5–6 minutes) from first
principles. Keep two questions separate:

does changing the order change the
measured outcome, and does

the proposed search method beat a matched
alternative at the

same distinct-evaluation budget? Present
the five audit questions as a

scientific checklist: Does ordering
produce meaningful fitness variance? Is

evaluation deterministic or sufficiently
averaged? Is exact ground truth

known for small instances? Is random
sampling compared at the

same distinct-evaluation budget? Are
headline claims supported by exact

enumeration or at least 40 seeds with
intervals? Define all

metrics visually: fitness distribution;
optimum density; distinct

evaluations; hit rate; regret; Wilson
interval for proportions; bootstrap

interval for mean evaluations; Pearson
versus Spearman correlation. Use one

numerical micro-example for hit rate and
regret before beginning the

experiment ledger. The distinction is part
of the result. A

large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
